Chaim Weizmann is a chemist. As a biochemist, Weizmann is considered to be the 'father' of industrial fermentation.
What is the atomic number of Hydrogen?
Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
In what year was Ted Kaczynski born?
Ted Kaczynski: The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM (University and Airline Bombing) before his identity was known, resulting in the media naming him the "Unabomber".
In what year was Uranium discovered?
Uranium is a chemical element; it has symbol U and atomic number 92.
In what year was Cobalt discovered?
Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
Ciprofloxacin: Pfizer. Ciprofloxacin, sold under the brand name Cipro among others, is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat a number of bacterial infections.
In which country did the Junkers Ju 87 take place?
Junkers Ju 87: Germany. The Junkers Ju 87, popularly known as the "Stuka", is a German dive bomber and ground-attack aircraft.
Who is credited with discovering Iodine?
Iodine: Bernard Courtois. Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
Who is credited with discovering Mendelevium?
Mendelevium: Glenn Theodore Seaborg. Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101.
Who is credited with discovering Magnesium?
Magnesium: Joseph Black. Magnesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Mg and atomic number 12.
This tall wetland monocot, also known as muskrat root, may be toxic if ingested and has no proven clinical benefit despite traditional medicinal use — which plant?
Acorus calamus (also called sweet flag, sway or muskrat root, among many other common names) is a species of flowering plant with psychoactive chemicals.
Ranging from South Florida to Peru, this reptile is the most widespread member of its family in the Americas and one of only two species that commonly thrive in saltwater — which species?
American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus) is a species of crocodilian found in the Neotropics.
NATO codenamed 'Curl' and nicknamed 'Nastia' in the USSR, this twin-engine turboprop transport was later license-built in China as the Xi'an Y-7 — what is it?

Antonov An-26 (NATO reporting name: Curl, nicknamed Nastia in the USSR) is a twin-engined turboprop regional airliner and military transport aircraft, designed and produced in the Soviet Union from 1969 to 1986.
Part of the family Ericaceae, these shrubs flower in April and May in the Northern Hemisphere and October and November south of the equator — what are they called?
Azalea (-) are flowering shrubs in the genus Rhododendron, particularly the former subgenera Tsutsusi (evergreen) and Pentanthera (deciduous).

This scientific discipline, a hybrid of chemistry and biology, studies the chemical processes occurring within living organisms and is generally divided into structural biology, enzymology, and metabolism — what's the field called?
Biochemistry (distinct from chemical biology), is the study of chemical processes within and relating to living organisms.
Whose book Atlas of the Heart became an HBO Max documentary series in 2022, following an earlier Netflix film about her work on courage?
Brené Brown (born November 18, 1965) is an American academic, author and podcaster.
First classified by Linnaeus in 1753, which herbaceous annual takes its specific name from the Latin for 'cultivated' and has long supplied fiber, seed oil, food and medicine?
Cannabis sativa is an annual herbaceous flowering plant.
Sometimes called melde or wild spinach, this weedy annual plant is often distinguished from its relatives in the same genus as the 'white' goosefoot — which plant?
Chenopodium album is a fast-growing annual plant in the flowering plant family Amaranthaceae.

Native to Australasia and ranging from the Philippines to the Solomon Islands, these 21 parrot species are recognizable by their prominent crests and curved bills, with plumage that's mostly white, grey, or black — name the group?
Cockatoo is any of the 21 species of parrots belonging to the family Cacatuidae, the only family in the superfamily Cacatuoidea, native to Australasia.
Which compound acts as a cellular buffer and, via its phosphorylated form, hands phosphate groups back to ADP to recharge ATP in muscle and brain?
Creatine (or) is an organic compound that, in vertebrates, facilitates recycling of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), primarily in muscle and brain tissue.

Generally moving particles, energy, or other quantities from regions of higher concentration to lower, this stochastic physical process is driven by a gradient in Gibbs free energy and can occasionally even run 'uphill' via spinodal decomposition — name this process?
Diffusion is the net movement of anything (for example, atoms, ions, molecules, energy) generally from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

This order of about 1,000 predatory fish species undergoes dramatic transformation from a distinctive larval stage to its adult form, and includes roughly 20 different families — what are these long, snake-like fish called?
Eel are ray-finned fish belonging to the order Anguilliformes, which consists of eight suborders, 20 families, 164 genera, and about 1000 species.

Combining lab and field science with strong ties to ecology and evolutionary biology, this discipline earned three of its founders a shared 1973 Nobel Prize for their work on animal behavior — what field is it?
Ethology is a branch of zoology that studies the behaviour of non-human animals.
Using a skin membrane called a patagium plus a long tail for steering, these gliding rodents can sail from tree to tree without true flight — what are they called?
Flying squirrel (scientifically known as Pteromyini or Petauristini) are a tribe of 50 species of squirrels in the family Sciuridae.

Sharing the 1988 Nobel Prize, this American biochemist pioneered rational drug design — studying a drug's target rather than relying on trial and error — and her work led to AZT, the first widely used AIDS drug. Who was she?
Gertrude B. Elion (January 23, 1918 - February 21, 1999) was an American biochemist and pharmacologist, who shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with George H. Hitchings.
Named from Ancient Greek words for 'blood' and 'to make,' this biological process produces up to a hundred billion new blood cells per day in a healthy adult — what is it?
Haematopoiesis (from Ancient Greek (hama) 'blood' and (poien) 'to make'; also hematopoiesis in US English, sometimes h(a)emopoiesis) is the formation of blood cellular components.

Discovered in 2013 deep in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, this archaic human left behind over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, yet a tiny brain keeps its place in our family tree a puzzle — what species is it?

Homo naledi is an extinct species of archaic human discovered in 2013 in the Rising Star Cave system, Gauteng province, South Africa, part of the Cradle of Humankind, dating back to the Middle Pleistocene 335,000-236,000 years ago.

A leading figure among Israel's 'New Historians,' this scholar characterizes the 1948 Palestinian expulsion as a deliberate campaign in his research and now teaches at the University of Exeter — who is he?
Ilan Pappé (born 7 November 1954) is an Israeli historian and political scientist, known for his work on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and as a leading figure among the New Historians.
An economist-turned-pundit who rose to fame on Argentine TV talk shows, who became the nation's 57th president in 2023 under the banner La Libertad Avanza?
Javier Milei (born 22 October 1970) is an Argentine politician and economist who has served as the 57th president of Argentina since 2023.
Arrested in 1995 for various computer crimes and imprisoned for five years, this convicted hacker later became a computer-security consultant and author — who is he?
Kevin Mitnick (August 6, 1963 - July 16, 2023) was an American computer security consultant, author, and convicted hacker.
Sometimes a side effect of medication or an alcohol interaction, which state of sluggishness and low motivation usually resolves with rest and better nutrition?
Lethargy is a state of physical or mental weariness, fatigue, sluggishness, or lack of energy.
Often caused by cigarette smoking or inhaled chemicals damaging airway cell DNA, this malignant tumor often shows no symptoms until it has already spread. What disease is it?
Lung cancer is a malignant tumor that originates in the tissues of the lungs.

This prehistoric proboscidean's molars have ridge-like zygodont cusps very different from a mammoth's, and its genus diverged from elephant ancestors over 28 million years ago in the Oligocene — which animal?

Mastodon (from Ancient Greek (masts) 'breast' and (odos) 'tooth') is a member of the genus Mammut (German for 'mammoth'), which was endemic to North America and lived from the late Miocene to the early Holocene.
Carrying the NATO reporting name 'Halo,' this Soviet/Russian heavy transport helicopter is the largest of its kind ever to enter serial production — name the aircraft?
Mil Mi-26 is a Soviet/Russian heavy transport helicopter.

Caused when fly larvae burrow into and feed on an animal's tissue, this parasitic infestation is triggered by open wounds but can occur on unbroken skin when species such as the botfly are involved — name this condition?
Myiasis (my-), also known as flystrike or fly strike, is the parasitic infestation of the body of a live animal by fly larvae (maggots) that grow inside the host while feeding on its tissue.

Introduced in 2001 and operated by the U.S. Air Force, this high-altitude, remotely piloted surveillance aircraft uses synthetic aperture radar and infrared sensors for long-endurance reconnaissance missions — name the aircraft?

Northrop Grumman RQ-4 Global Hawk is a high-altitude, remotely-piloted surveillance aircraft introduced in 2001. It was initially designed by Ryan Aeronautical (now part of Northrop Grumman), and known as Tier II+ during development.
This bivalve mollusk is prized both as a delicacy on the half shell and, in certain species, for the pearls it produces inside its shell — what is it?
Oyster is the common name for a number of different families of salt-water bivalve molluscs that live in marine or brackish habitats.

Nicknamed with the backronym 'Practical Extraction and Reporting Language,' this dynamic scripting language was developed by Larry Wall in 1987 and borrows features from C, AWK, and sed — which language?
Perl is a high-level, general-purpose, interpreted, dynamic programming language.
A large, rounded body that orbits a star but isn't one itself — by the strictest definition, the Solar System has eight of these — what are they called?
Planet is a large, rounded astronomical body that is generally required to be in orbit around a star, stellar remnant, or brown dwarf, and is not one itself.
This sense of self-movement, force, and body position is mediated by receptors located within muscles, tendons, and joints — what is it called?
Proprioception (--) is the sense of self-movement, force, and body position. Proprioception ( PROH-pree-oh-SEP-shən, -⁠ə-) is the sense of self-movement, force, and body position.
Distinguished from its smaller relative the crow mainly by size, this large-bodied passerine bird genus includes the common and thick-billed species, the biggest passerines alive — what bird is it?
Raven is any of several large-bodied passerine bird species in the genus Corvus.
Created by Yukihiro 'Matz' Matsumoto in 1990s Japan, this dynamically typed programming language treats absolutely everything — even primitive data types — as an object — what's the language?
Ruby (programming language) is a general-purpose programming language designed with an emphasis on programming productivity and simplicity.
This taxonomic order groups cephalopods distinguished by having ten arms instead of eight — what order is it?
Sepiida is an order of ten-armed cephalopods.
Found throughout the nightshade family — including in potato leaves, fruit, and tubers — this saponin-family toxin doubles as the plant's own natural pesticide. What compound is it?
Solanine is a glycoalkaloid poison found in species of the nightshade family within the genus Solanum, such as the potato (Solanum tuberosum).
Generated in mitochondria via the TCA cycle, this dicarboxylic compound gets converted into fumarate by an enzyme that helps build ATP — which molecule?
Succinic acid is a dicarboxylic acid with the chemical formula (CH2)2(CO2H)2.
This group of inherited blood disorders reduces the body's hemoglobin production, sometimes causing anemia, an enlarged spleen, and stunted growth in children — what condition is it?
Thalassemia are a group of inherited blood disorders that manifest as the production of reduced hemoglobin.

This invasive annual plant, native to warm regions of Eurasia and Africa but now found in North America and Australia, produces small woody burrs with sharp spines capable of piercing bare feet. What plant is this?
Tribulus terrestris is an annual plant in the caltrop family (Zygophyllaceae) widely distributed around the world.
First glimpsed in 1892 through tobacco-plant disease and counted as the most numerous biological entity on Earth, this submicroscopic agent can only replicate inside a living cell. What is it?
Virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside the living cells of an organism.
Almost always found combined with lanthanide minerals and never on its own in nature, this element with symbol Y is a key ingredient in the phosphors used inside LEDs — which element?
Yttrium is a chemical element; it has symbol Y and atomic number 39.
A pseudoscientific but ancient component of traditional Chinese medicine, this practice involves inserting thin needles into the body, most often for pain relief — what is it called?
Coined in 1852 but now considered stigmatizing in clinical settings, this WHO-estimated 283-million-person global condition involves continued drinking despite the harm it causes — what is it called?
Used to treat dangerous heart rhythms like ventricular fibrillation, which drug can take weeks to work when swallowed but carries risks of lung, liver, thyroid, and eye toxicity?
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois won the 2003 Nobel Prize for pioneering work on superfluidity and the quantum physics of low-temperature helium — who was he?
Known as mugwort or wormwood, this daisy-family plant has long been used for both medicinal and culinary purposes — what species is it?

Artemisia vulgaris: Medicinal plant known as common mugwort. It is one of several species in the genus Artemisia commonly known as mugwort, although Artemisia vulgaris is the species most often called mugwort.
Blooming for weeks each spring and thriving in the shade under trees, these flowering shrubs belong to the genus Rhododendron — what are they called?
Azalea: Subgroup of rhododendron flowering shrubs.
A likely hybrid of lemon and a bitter citrus relative, this fragrant fruit flavors tea, snus, and perfume, though it can heighten skin's sensitivity to sunlight — which fruit?
Credited with kicking off the Jet Age, this swept-wing quadjet airliner entered regular passenger service with Pan Am in October 1958 — which aircraft?

He won a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics for an effect he discovered as a Cambridge PhD student in 1962 — then, in the 1970s, took up Transcendental Meditation and pursued ideas beyond mainstream science. Who is he?
Its dihydrate form is the mineral gypsum and its dehydrated cousin is bassanite; sparingly soluble, it causes permanent hardness in water — which inorganic salt is this?
Calcium sulfate: Chemical derived from gypsum used in food and industry.
A nerve compression syndrome caused when the median nerve in the wrist becomes compressed, causing numbness and tingling in the thumb and fingers. What is this condition?
Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve in the wrist. It can also be measured with electrodiagnostic tests.
India's third lunar mission carried a lander named Vikram and a rover, both replacing equivalents lost when the previous mission crashed on landing. What was the rover called?

Chandrayaan-3 is the third mission in ISRO's Chandrayaan lunar-exploration programme, consisting of the lander Vikram and the rover Pragyan, replacements for the equivalents on Chandrayaan-2, which crashed on landing.
In this chronic liver condition, healthy tissue is replaced by scar tissue and regenerative nodules, choking blood flow and causing portal hypertension — what is it called?
Cirrhosis: Chronic disease of the liver, characterized by fibrosis.
In this prolonged state of deep unconsciousness, a person cannot be awakened, shows no normal sleep-wake cycle, and may even be induced deliberately during general anesthesia — what is it?
Coma: State of unconsciousness. The person may experience respiratory and circulatory problems due to the body's inability to maintain normal bodily functions.
Smelling of vanilla but tasting bitter, which plant compound isn't itself an anticoagulant, though its derivatives inspired the blood-thinning drug warfarin?
This Zambian-born economist turned heads with four New York Times bestsellers, including "Dead Aid," which argues that foreign aid actually holds Africa back. Which author and life peer is it?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo: Zambian-born economist (born February 1969)
Known for feigning death when cornered, which genus of cat-sized marsupials includes the only marsupial species found north of Mexico?
Didelphis: Genus of marsupials. The six species in the genus Didelphis, commonly known as Large American opossums, are members of the opossum order, Didelphimorphia.
Nicknamed 'Viking disease,' this hand condition — first surgically treated in 1831 by the surgeon it's named after — permanently curls the ring finger inward. What is it?
Dupuytren's contracture: Medical condition featuring permanent bending of fingers.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit measures a material's ability to store electrical charge, equal to one coulomb per volt — what is it?
Farad: SI unit of electric capacitance.
Patented in 1962 and sold under a brand name synonymous with 'roofies,' this benzodiazepine is notoriously linked to date-rape drug use — what is it?
Flunitrazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Flunitrazepam, sold under the brand name Rohypnol among others, is a benzodiazepine used to treat severe insomnia and assist with anesthesia.
Born in Pisa in 1564, this Italian polymath has been crowned the father of observational astronomy and the scientific method — and was among the earliest tinkerers to build a thermoscope. Who is he?
Galileo Galilei: Italian physicist and astronomer (1564–1642)

This Italian friar and cosmological theorist proposed that stars were distant suns with their own planets, and was tried for heresy by the Roman Inquisition for insisting the universe is infinite — who was he?
Giordano Bruno: Italian Dominican friar, philosopher and mathematician (1548–1600)
This junctional area between the torso and thigh, where the lower abdominal wall meets the leg, is commonly strained in a familiar sports injury — what is it called?
Groin: Area between the torso and the thigh. In human anatomy, the groin, also known as the inguinal region or iliac region, is the junctional area between the torso and the thigh.

In 2018 this Chinese biophysicist announced the world's first gene-edited human babies — twin girls modified for HIV resistance — which got him onto Time's influential list and fired from his university. Who was he?
This academic discipline studies the methods, sources, and interpretive approaches historians use when writing about the past — what's it called?
Historiography: Study of the methods used by historians.
Defined as a blood level above 5.5 mmol/L, this elevated-potassium condition can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm and even cardiac arrest — what is it called?
Hyperkalemia: Excess potassium in the blood. Normal potassium levels are between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L (3.5 and 5.0 mEq/L) with levels above 5.5 mmol/L defined as hyperkalemia.

ISO 56000:2020 defines it as "a new or changed entity, realizing or redistributing value" — but the everyday version is the practical implementation of ideas, the cousin of invention focused on newness, improvement, and the spread of technologies. What's the word?
Innovation: Practical implementation of improvements. Innovation is the practical implementation of ideas that result in the creation or improvements of goods or services.
The first woman to chair the Federal Reserve, this American economist later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — who is she?
Janet Yellen: American economist and government official (born 1946)
Also known as the English or Persian walnut, this tree species native to Eurasia is cultivated worldwide, with China as its leading producer today — what is it?
Juglans regia: Species of tree (walnut). Juglans regia, known by various common names including the common walnut, English walnut, or Persian walnut amongst other names, is a species of walnut.

Ranked alongside Aristotle and Frege among history's most significant logicians, this thinker proved his completeness theorem in his 1929 Vienna dissertation before publishing his famous incompleteness theorems two years later — who is he?
Kurt Gödel: Mathematical logician and philosopher.
Often called the last physicist to master every branch of the field, this Soviet scientist co-discovered the density matrix method and developed the theory of superfluidity — who is he?
Nicknamed the sea devil, frogfish, or fishing frog, this species anchors a major commercial fishery in the Irish Sea and ranges from the Barents Sea to the Mediterranean — which fish?
Lophius piscatorius: Species of fish. Lophius piscatorius, commonly known as the angler, toadfish, sea frog, fishing frog, frogfish, or sea devil, is a species of Lophius in the family Lophiidae.
Males of this widespread dabbling duck species sport iridescent green heads, while females have brown-speckled plumage — which bird?
Mallard: Species of duck. The mallard or wild duck (Anas platyrhynchos) is a dabbling duck that breeds throughout the temperate and subtropical Americas, Eurasia, and North Africa.
Distinguished by its darker camouflage, conformal fuel tanks, and a two-seat cockpit, this all-weather multirole fighter first flew in 1986 for long-range interdiction missions — what is it?
McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle: American all-weather multirole fighter aircraft.
First made in 1969 and approved for medical use in 1978, this selective beta blocker treats high blood pressure, angina, and helps prevent migraines — what is it called?
Metoprolol: Beta blocker medication. It is also used to prevent further heart problems after myocardial infarction and to prevent headaches in those with migraines.
With velvety fur, tiny eyes, and powerful digging forelimbs, this subterranean mammal aerates garden soil and feasts on earthworms and slugs despite being seen as a pest — what is it?
Mole (animal): Common name for several small mammals.
One of the smallest self-replicating organisms known, this cell-wall-lacking bacterium was originally called the 'Eaton agent' after being cultivated in chicken eggs in 1944 — what organism is it?
Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Species of bacterium. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a species of very small-cell bacteria that lack a cell wall, in the class Mollicutes.

Published in the Principia Mathematica, this principle holds that every particle in the cosmos attracts every other with a pull proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the squared distance between them — which principle is it?
Newton's law of universal gravitation: Classical statement of gravity as force.

This family within the superfamily Delphinoidea includes species with 'whale' in their common names, like the pilot and false killer types, and ranges up in size to the massive orca — what is this family called?
Oceanic dolphin: Family of marine mammals.

Triggered by a surge of luteinizing hormone near the midpoint of the menstrual cycle, this event sees the ovarian follicle rupture and release an egg — which breaks down in under a day if it isn't fertilized. What is it called?
Ovulation: Release of egg cells from the ovaries.
This Stanford biologist became famous — and controversial — for his 1968 book warning that runaway population growth would bring famine and resource depletion. Who was he?
This inherited metabolic disorder, caused by mutations in the PAH gene, leaves patients unable to break down a certain amino acid and can give off a musty odor if untreated — what is it?
Phenylketonuria: Amino acid metabolic disorder. Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism that results in decreased metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine.
First classified as its own fossil order in 1835, this group of Mesozoic marine reptiles thrived through the Jurassic before dying out at the end of the Cretaceous — what are they called?
Plesiosaur: Order of reptiles (fossil). The Plesiosauria or plesiosaurs are an order or clade of extinct Mesozoic marine reptiles, belonging to the Sauropterygia.
This New World family within the order Carnivora encompasses raccoons, ringtails, coatis, and kinkajous, most of them omnivorous — what family is it?
Procyonidae: Family of mammals. Procyonidae ( PROH-see-ON-i-dee) is a New World family of the order Carnivora.
Native to southern China, this pear tree's fruit goes by dozens of names worldwide - Asian pear, apple pear, nashi pear - but is rarely baked into pies due to its high water content - which species?
Pyrus pyrifolia: Species of pear with round crisp grainy fruit.
Rooted in Minangkabau cooking at the crossroads of the Malacca Strait, this dish slow-cooks meat in spiced coconut milk until the oil separates and it fries in its own glaze — what is it?

Nicknamed the 'dark lady of DNA,' this X-ray crystallographer's crucial contributions to the discovery of DNA's structure went largely unrecognized in her lifetime — James Watson believed she'd have won a Nobel Prize had she lived. Who was she?
Also called Besnier–Boeck–Schaumann disease, this non-infectious condition forms clusters of inflammatory cells called granulomata, often starting in the lungs, skin, or lymph nodes — what is it?
Sarcoidosis: Abnormal formation of clumps of inflammatory cells (granulomata)
About 90% of this mood-regulating neurotransmitter is actually made in your gut, where it controls intestinal movement, rather than the brain — also known as 5-HT, what is it?
Serotonin: Monoamine neurotransmitter. It is involved in mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, and physiological processes such as vomiting and vasoconstriction.
With the formula CH3COONa, this colorless, moisture-absorbing compound is the salt formed from acetic acid — what is it called?
Named in 1880 from Greek words meaning 'bunch of grapes,' this genus of spherical, grape-clustered bacteria can grow with or without oxygen — which genus?
Among the largest flighted birds in their range, these waterfowl of genus Cygnus typically mate for life and lay three to eight eggs per clutch — what are they?
Swan: Tribe of large water birds.
Made of collagen like its bone-to-bone cousin the ligament, this tough band of connective tissue instead links muscle to bone, and there are about 4,000 of them in your body — what is it called?
Tendon: Type of tissue that connects muscle to bone.
Native to Africa and the Middle East, this freshwater fish has become a global aquaculture staple but can turn invasive in warm habitats like Australia — which fish?
Tilapia: Common name for many species of fish.
This essential amino acid, which the body can't make on its own, is a precursor to serotonin, melatonin, and vitamin B3 — which amino acid?
Found in Central and South America, only three living species of this blood-feeding, leaf-nosed flying mammal exist, while two extinct relatives once roamed North America — which creature?

The smallest member of this genus, found in Great Britain, is also considered the tiniest carnivorous mammal species on Earth, with some populations turning white in winter. What group of small predators is this?
Weasel: Mammal of the mustelid family.
Known to TV audiences as 'Dr. Now,' this Iranian-born American surgeon has spent over a decade helping patients on My 600-lb Life reach life-saving weight loss — who is he?
Younan Nowzaradan: Iranian-American surgeon, television personality, and author (born 1944)
Arsenic is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for arsenic is As. Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
What is the chemical symbol for nihonium?
The symbol for nihonium is Nh. Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.

In what year was Ranbir Kapoor born?
Ranbir Kapoor: Ranbir Raj Kapoor (pronounced [ɾəɳˈbiːɾ kəˈpuːɾ]; born 28 September 1982) is an Indian actor who works in Hindi-language films.
In what year was Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh born?
Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh (Edward Antony Richard Louis; born 10 March 1964), is a member of the British royal family.
In what year was Brooklyn Beckham born?
Brooklyn Beckham: Brooklyn Joseph Peltz Beckham (né Beckham; born 4 March 1999) is a British-American media personality.
In what year was Neve Campbell born?
Neve Campbell: Neve Adrianne Campbell (born October 3, 1973) is a Canadian actress.
In what year was Tom Hanks born?
Tom Hanks: Thomas Jeffrey Hanks (born July 9, 1956) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Nicola Peltz born?
Nicola Peltz: Nicola Anne Peltz Beckham (née Peltz; born January 9, 1995) is an American actress.
In what year was Rob Lowe born?
Rob Lowe: Robert Hepler Lowe (born March 17, 1964) is an American actor, filmmaker, and entertainment host.
In what year was Charlie Hunnam born?
Charlie Hunnam: Charles Matthew Hunnam (born 10 April 1980) is an English actor.
In what year was Keanu Reeves born?
Keanu Reeves: Keanu Charles Reeves ( kee-AH-noo; born September 2, 1964) is a Canadian actor and musician.
In what year was Harvey Weinstein born?
Harvey Weinstein (born March 19, 1952) is an American former film producer and convicted sex offender.
In what year was Megan Fox born?
Megan Fox: Megan Denise Fox (born May 16, 1986) is an American actress.
In what year did Philip Seymour Hoffman die?
Philip Seymour Hoffman (July 23, 1967 – February 2, 2014) was an American actor.
In what year did Robert Redford die?
Robert Redford: Redford began his career on television in the late 1950s, appearing in anthology series such as Alfred Hitchcock Presents and The Twilight Zone.
